To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) sequencing of selected exons of the DNAH 5 and DNAI 1 genes in PCD patients is a reasonable first step to detect mutations, (ii) it is necessary to take into account the phenotype, (iii) it is necessary for the laboratory to be able to perform sequencing of the whole DNAH 5 gene if the first step fails, (iv) the sensitivity of the first step is 62.5%
the sequencing of selected exons of the DNAH and DNAI1 genes is a cost-effective approach in the diagnosis of PCD.

the sequencing of selected 9 DNAH5 and four DNAI1 exons is effective in the detection of PCD mutations and that it can be recommended for the routine diagnostic testing of PCD in the Czech population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a group of patients with a rare genetic disorder.
the genetic background of PCD in a Czech population, and it may be helpful in the genetic counselling and diagnosis of PCD patients.
the genetic background of PCD, its clinical presentation and its treatment in the Czech Republic.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
selected exon sequencing of DNAH5 is a useful first step for the diagnosis of PCD in the Czech population.
the selected exon sequencing is a good screening method for PCD mutations.

selected exon sequencing of DNAH5/DNAI1 is not sensitive enough in all patients with PCD to identify the causative mutation(s), but it may be a good starting point to identify the most likely causative gene(s).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
selected exon sequencing detects at most one mutated allele in about one-third of patients who have P CD due to DNAH 5 or DNAI 1 mutations.

the sequencing of selected exons is a useful tool in the diagnostic work-up of PCD, and the sequencing of 13 exons of DNAI1 and DNAH5 genes is sufficient for the diagnosis in a majority of patients with PCD due to mutations in these genes.
we have shown that the DNAH5 and the DNAI1 mutations are the most common genetic cause of PCD in our population.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the DNAH5 mutations are more frequent in the Czech PDC patients, and they are not restricted to the exons 43 and 46, as described in other populations.
the sequencing of selected exons of the DNAH 5 gene can detect mutations in 62.5% of patients with PCD, and the sequencing of all exonic regions of the DNAI1 gene in 25%.
targeted genetic testing of DNAH5/ DNAI1 is a reasonable approach to identify patients with PCD, especially when phenotype is taken into consideration.
